title: Introducing Alternate Clouds: Decentralized Infrastructure for Services and Agent Swarms
excerpt: Alternate Clouds gives teams one web and CLI workflow for deploying application services and coordinated AI agent swarms on decentralized infrastructure.
content: Cloud platforms made deployment easier, but they also concentrated applications, billing, and operational control inside a small number of vendors. Distributed compute creates more infrastructure choice, yet raw capacity alone does not give a team a usable product experience.
**Alternate Clouds is the deployment platform from Alternate Futures.** It brings application services and coordinated AI agent swarms into one project-centered workflow.
## Why decentralized infrastructure?

A useful decentralized cloud should make infrastructure choices visible without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure operator. Teams should be able to select resources, regions, and workload controls while the platform handles deployment state, health, logs, access, and billing.
The goal is practical control:
- **Infrastructure choice** -- deploy workloads across independent compute providers
- **Workload portability** -- describe the service instead of rebuilding it around one vendor
- **Operational visibility** -- keep deployments, logs, health, networking, and spend in one place
- **Guarded autonomy** -- give agent teams models and tools through explicit policy and budget controls
## What ships in open beta
Alternate Clouds supports several workload paths through the same service model:
| Workload | Deployment path |
| Application services | Templates, GitHub repositories, Docker images, functions, or empty servers |
| GPU workloads | Services configured with explicit compute, GPU, and region requirements |
| Confidential services | Workloads placed on confidential compute when the service requires it |
| Agent swarms | Multi-agent teams with sequential, parallel, loop, supervisor, handoff, or graph topologies |

Every service lives inside a project and uses the same core operational surfaces. Swarms add a Source editor for agents and topology, version history, a private chat room, optional Discord channels, and per-run inference cost visibility.
## One platform, two paths
The web app starts with **New Service**. Choose a service type, configure its source and resources, then deploy from the shared service workspace.
The CLI exposes the same service workflow:
```bash
npm install -g @alternatefutures/acc
acc login
acc projects create --name my-project
acc services create
acc services deploy
For a swarm, the workflow adds local authoring and testing before the cloud deployment:
```bash
acc swarms init my-swarm && cd my-swarm
acc add agent
acc add swarm
acc run review --input "Say hello in one sentence."
acc swarms deploy review --yes
acc run review --remote --input "Say hello in one sentence."

By default, local and deployed swarms call supported models through the platform and charge usage to the organization. A team does not need to paste a model-provider secret to complete the standard flow.
## Why swarms matter

A single agent can handle a bounded task. A swarm can divide work among named agents, run them in a defined topology, and preserve a visible record of who ran, what it cost, and whether the run succeeded. That makes multi-agent work something a team can operate rather than a collection of prompts held together by convention.
Deployed swarms can answer in their private end-to-end-encrypted room or in connected Discord channels. Tools remain off by default and are granted through reviewed policy.
## Open beta
Alternate Clouds is now in open beta. [Join the open beta](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) to deploy a service or build your first agent team.
The decentralized cloud becomes useful when deploying and operating on it feels ordinary.

title: How to Deploy Your First AI Agent Swarm on Alternate Clouds
excerpt: Create an agent team, test it locally, deploy it to decentralized compute, and run it through the Alternate Clouds CLI.
content: Alternate Clouds lets you define a team of named agents, choose how they work together, test the team locally, and deploy the same swarm to decentralized compute. This guide follows the production-proven open-beta workflow.
> The standard path does not require a model-provider secret. Local and deployed runs use the platform's inference service and charge usage to your organization. Bringing your own key is optional.
## Prerequisites
- An Alternate Futures account
- The current Alternate Clouds CLI
- An organization with enough wallet balance for inference and the deployment lease
## 1. Install and sign in
```bash
npm install -g @alternatefutures/acc
cd ~ && acc login
acc whoami
The login command opens a browser for approval. The final command confirms which account the CLI will use.
## 2. Create a project
```bash
cd ~ && acc projects create --name my-swarm-project
You can switch between existing projects later with `acc projects switch`. Every swarm command uses the active project unless you pass `--project` explicitly.
## 3. Initialize the swarm
```bash
cd ~
acc swarms init my-swarm
cd my-swarm
This creates `swarm.toml` and the project folders used for agent definitions and personas.
## 4. Add an agent and a team
```bash
acc add agent
acc add swarm

The first wizard asks for the agent's one-word name, job, and model. The second asks for a team name, topology, and members. Choose the sequential topology for a simple first run. In the examples below, the agent is named `researcher` and the team is named `review`.
Supported topologies include sequential, parallel with a reducer, loop, supervisor, handoff, and custom graph connections.
## 5. Test locally
```bash
acc run review --input "Say hello in one sentence."
The swarm runtime executes on your machine while the model request goes through Alternate Clouds. Use `acc dev` when you want the local inspector and model diagnostics.
## 6. Deploy
```bash
acc swarms deploy review --yes
acc swarms status review

The platform compiles the saved definition, resolves the released runtime, creates the runtime secrets and policy material, reserves compute capacity, and waits for the runtime to register. The swarm is ready when status reports `ACTIVE` and `runtime_ready: true`.

Only one deployment of a swarm can run at a time. An unchanged deploy reports `Nothing changed`; after changing the model, definition, or channel map, stop the existing deployment before deploying again.
## 7. Run it in the cloud
```bash
acc run review --remote --input "Draft a short launch checklist."
A successful run returns the answer, run identifier, and cost. The cost combines model usage and the deployment lease; runs also appear in the service's inference spend view.
## 8. Join the private room
```bash
acc swarms room review
acc chat join chat.alternatefutures.ai

The first command prints the room's six-word passphrase. Inside the room, `@researcher` addresses one agent and `@all` runs the whole swarm. A message without a mention runs nothing and costs nothing.
Every deployed swarm gets one private end-to-end-encrypted room. The bridge that speaks for the agents runs inside the swarm deployment and is scoped to that swarm.
## 9. Operate and stop
```bash
acc swarms logs review --tail 200
acc swarms stop review
Tools are off by default and must be granted through reviewed policy. Stopping the swarm closes its lease and stops the compute charge.
## Web app path

The same workflow is available without installing the CLI: create or open a project, choose **New Service > Swarm**, add the agents and topology on **Source**, save the definition, and deploy from the footer. The Source tab also manages the private room, Discord connections, and version history.

title: The Web3 Infrastructure Gap: Why Decentralized Compute Needs an Application Layer
excerpt: Decentralized compute has capacity. What application teams still need is a usable layer for deploying services and operating AI agent swarms.
content: Decentralized infrastructure has spent years proving that independent providers can supply storage, CPUs, GPUs, and confidential compute. The harder product problem now sits one layer higher: how does an application team use that capacity without assembling its own cloud platform?
## The gap is operational
Teams that want alternatives to a single cloud vendor still face three incomplete choices:
- **Centralized application platforms** provide a polished workflow but keep deployment, billing, and availability inside one vendor
- **Raw compute marketplaces** provide capacity but leave service configuration, secrets, networking, health, logs, and lifecycle management to the customer
- **Agent frameworks** help define behavior but usually stop before deployment, model billing, policy, recovery, and multi-agent operations
The missing layer is not another marketplace. It is an application platform that turns distributed capacity into services a team can deploy and operate.
## AI raises the bar

AI workloads make the application layer more important. A production agent may need a model, durable state, a tool policy, an execution budget, a private place to receive work, and an audit trail. A multi-agent swarm adds topology, versioning, per-agent identity, coordination, and per-run cost.
Raw infrastructure does not provide those product-level controls by itself.
> Decentralized compute becomes useful to application teams when the operational experience is as coherent as the infrastructure beneath it is distributed.
## What the application layer should provide
Alternate Clouds brings the current product surface into one project and service model.
### For application services
- Create services from templates, GitHub repositories, Docker images, functions, or empty servers
- Choose compute, storage, GPU, region, budget, and runtime controls
- Inspect deployment state, health, logs, networking, and spend from one workspace
- Use the web app for guided setup or the `acc` CLI for repeatable workflows
### For agent swarms
- Define named agents and choose how they work together
- Test the same team locally before deploying it to the cloud
- Run sequential, parallel, loop, supervisor, handoff, or graph topologies
- Give each deployed swarm a private encrypted room and optional Discord channels
- Track model usage, lease cost, run status, and service spend
- Keep tools off by default and grant them through explicit policy
### For operators
- Manage services and swarms inside the same project model
- Route model calls through the platform by default or bring an organization or project key
- Stop a workload to close its lease and end the compute charge
- Keep the provider-specific mechanics behind a consistent deployment surface
## What decentralized should mean

Decentralization is not a badge. It changes where workloads run, how capacity is selected, what can fail, and how recovery works. Those choices should be visible to the operator without becoming the developer's full-time job.
That is the application-layer opportunity: preserve infrastructure choice while making deployment, policy, communication, and cost legible.
## The open-beta test

Alternate Clouds is testing that proposition now with application services and deployable agent swarms. A user can build a team in the web app or CLI, run it locally, deploy it, talk to it in a private room, connect a Discord channel, inspect cost, and stop the lease from the same platform.
[Join the open beta](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) and tell us where the application layer still gets in your way.

title: I Set Out to Write Standards. I Ended Up Building a Cloud.
excerpt: Angela Steffens on why a human-alignment standards project turned into decentralized cloud infrastructure — and what Clouds can and cannot honestly claim today.
content: People look at what we do and find the shape confusing. A human-alignment platform. Also a cloud hosting company. Also an agent runtime. Pick a lane.
It's one lane. Here's the sentence that connects it: **you cannot set standards for technology you don't control the means of producing.**
That took me a couple of years and a rebrand to learn properly, so let me show the work.
## The gap I actually started with
The company was called Mold. As in: to shape. To form technology around a human impression, rather than pouring humans into a machine-shaped mold and calling what comes out progress.

The founding observation was narrow and, I still think, correct: *no standards body exists for the explicit purpose of aligning technology with humanity at a holistic level.* Not a piece of it. There are excellent people working on security. On accessibility. On HCI. On AI safety. They largely do not talk to each other, and the seams between them are where people get hurt.

The clearest example is security. Social engineering accounts for the overwhelming majority of breaches — and security remains almost entirely separate from interaction design. We treat the human as the vulnerability to be patched around, rather than the system to be designed for. You can't secure humans from outside human-centered design. That's not a slogan, it's an org chart problem with a body count.
So: three deliverables.
- **A decentralized, verifiable ledger** for research and training data.
- **An API for safe agentic transactions**, with settlement.

- **Linguistic benchmarks for dialect and regional variation** — because “works for everyone” currently means “works best for the English spoken by the people who built it,” and that is not fixable with good intentions. It requires architectural decisions, made early.
And what all three are building toward: a model per person.

Alignment is not one artifact. There is no single screen, default, policy, or model that is correctly aligned to everyone, because people are not one thing. We say “aligned to human values” as though humanity had submitted a single set. A system aligned to the average is misaligned with nearly everyone in particular, and the further you sit from whoever that average was computed over, the worse it serves you. The dialect benchmark is that same argument in miniature: “works for everyone” almost always means “works for the people who built it.”
So the endpoint isn’t a better universal model. It’s individualized ones — software interfaces, models included, shaped to the specific human using them.

Which is also why the alignment argument and the infrastructure argument are the same argument. A model per person is the exact opposite of one enormous model served to everybody from a handful of datacenters. It needs inference that is cheap, distributed, close to the person, and not owned by a company whose margin depends on centralizing it.
That's the platform — the Human Alignment Platform. It's still the point.
## Why that turned into infrastructure
Here's what I ran into.
![Four stacked layers — training data, compute, runtime, hardware — each labelled with who already owns it, bracketed as “not ours to set terms on”.](/images/layer-ownership.svg)

Standards without owned infrastructure are advisory. You can publish the most rigorous benchmark in the world, and if it runs on compute rented from the three companies whose behavior the benchmark exists to constrain, you have written a strongly worded letter, nothing more.

Every layer I needed was already someone's product. Training data was an asset on someone else's balance sheet. Compute was a line item priced by those same three companies' capacity planning. The software everyone builds on turned out to be a sales channel for the company giving it away. Every "open" agent framework I evaluated followed the same structure: open-source the framework, centralize the hosting, monetize the lock-in. And it ends the same way every time — acquired by a hyperscaler, or absorbed into one of the big closed labs. That's not a criticism of those companies. It's a rational business model with a predictable exit. It's just incompatible with anyone downstream setting terms, because the company you made your arrangement with is rarely the company that ends up holding it.
So we stopped waiting for that layer to exist and started building it.

That's the whole origin of the Clouds product. Not a pivot away from alignment. The realization that the alignment work has a hardware dependency, and nobody downstream of those business models was going to satisfy it for us.
## Agents made it urgent instead of theoretical

I've said publicly that the future of software companies is six to twelve people doing the work that used to take hundreds, assisted by agentic AI. I believe that, and we're running the experiment on ourselves — our marketing, code review, research, and design work is dispatched to a swarm of agents on our own infrastructure. It's the most honest product feedback loop I know. Every rough edge in the platform is one my own agents hit first.

What that surfaced: an agent that can't deploy is a chatbot. The moment an agent does real work it needs the same things a person would: somewhere to run, somewhere to put things, a way to prove who it is, money it's allowed to spend, and a line it isn't allowed to cross. And it needs them at a different scale — thousands of small jobs that start and finish in minutes, rather than a dozen big ones that run for months.

The big clouds will serve that, expensively, through systems built for a person clicking buttons with the machine version bolted on afterwards. We want the other thing: one command that works the same whether I type it or an agent calls it, and cheap enough that being wrong about how much you need isn't painful.

The software that runs our agents is open source, and it runs wherever you want it — your own laptop, your own servers, or ours. You can point it at whatever AI models you prefer: somebody else's, ours, or ones you run yourself. And everything the agent learns along the way is yours, and leaves with you when you go.

That last part matters more than it sounds. An agent's memory is the valuable thing it builds up — months of knowing how you work, what you've decided, what went wrong last time. If you can't take that with you, you don't own the agent. You're renting it. We made it portable on purpose, which means we have to compete on being good rather than on being hard to leave.
## Decentralized is a means, not a religion

I get sorted into the Web3 bucket, and fair enough — some of the pieces come from there. But I'm not building this because decentralization is virtuous. I'm building multi-provider infrastructure because single-provider dependency is the actual failure mode, and decentralized networks are the cheapest large pool of capacity nobody else is aggregating. We run on Akash. We also run on AWS. A customer who needs a hyperscaler region should get one, through us, without a lecture.

The savings are real: for the right workload shapes, 30–80% under hyperscaler list. They're genuinely absent for other shapes, and I say so, because a pricing claim without its conditions is a claim that gets me fired by the first customer who tests it.
## The furthest version of this argument is a building

If you take "own the means of production" seriously, you eventually run out of software to own. Underneath the runtime is a rack. Underneath the rack is a power contract, a jurisdiction, and someone else's siting decision.
![Two panels comparing cooling: a rack-scale GPU configuration requiring liquid and a supporting cooling plant, versus an air-cooled rack with airflow straight through.](/images/air-vs-liquid.svg)

So we're designing transportable, dedicated AI-inference modules — containerized datacenters — built around SambaNova's accelerator racks, in three sizes, for sites with a network connection and for sites deliberately cut off from the internet entirely. The thesis is unromantic: put dedicated inference capacity where the power actually is. Power that's stranded, constrained, cheap, or jurisdictionally controlled. We bring the software, the billing, and the customers. The module brings the floor.

They're air-cooled, and that's most of why we went to SambaNova instead of building around GPUs. The current generation of rack-scale GPU systems needs liquid cooling and the plant to support it. These racks don't — no liquid loop, no water running through them, just a sealed air path. For something you intend to truck to a site and set down next to a substation, that isn't a performance footnote. It's the difference between a product and a plumbing project.

I'm not claiming this silicon beats a GPU at everything; they're good at different halves of the job. I'm claiming one of them fits in a box I can put almost anywhere, and that constraint is doing more work in this design than any benchmark.

The other requirement is non-negotiable: you have to be able to run your own models on it. That sounds obvious until you start pricing accelerators, because plenty of very fast silicon quietly assumes you'll run the models the vendor has optimized and blessed. Hardware that only runs somebody else's approved model list is the same lock-in I've been describing this whole piece, with a power cord attached. If the argument is that you should own your stack, the metal has to honor it too — and holding that line has already cost us a design revision, which is what it looks like when a principle is real.

This is where sovereignty stops being a marketing word. A customer who owns the machine, on their own land, disconnected from the internet if they want, is not relying on my good intentions or my terms of service. They're relying on a physical fact. That's a different kind of promise, and it's the only kind I actually trust.

The buyers arriving for this are not hobbyists. They're utilities, public universities, Tribal entities, and agencies with a sovereignty mandate and no appetite for their inference running in somebody else's jurisdiction. I don't have to argue that the demand exists. I have to be honest about what we can serve today.

Now the parts that aren't true yet, because this is exactly the sort of project that invites rounding up. A recognized modular-data-center certification path exists; we have not completed it. The layout isn't frozen, so there are no delivery dates, no installed price, and no uptime or efficiency numbers — you don't get performance claims from a unit that hasn't been commissioned. It isn't off-grid: it's designed for site-specific on-site generation, which is a different sentence and a much smaller one. And these modules don't become low-power appliances when they're idle. The idle draw is real and it's material, which means utilization and workload economics belong in every honest conversation about them, including this one.

We intend to manufacture them in Olympia. That part isn't sentiment — it's a port, a light-industrial corridor, and an export route. But I'd be lying if I said the symmetry escaped me. I grew up downstream of a scene in this town that said, in all caps, in a zine assembled at two in the morning, that we must take over the means of production in order to create our own meanings. They couldn't. The pressing plant belonged to somebody else.

There's a town twenty minutes south of here where, when the bank failed in 1931, they printed their own money on the local newspaper's press. Wooden scrip, and they traded on it for two years. The press is still in the museum. It still works.
I'm trying to build the pressing plant in the same county.
## The loop
Which is exactly why the module isn't the product. The loop is.
![A four-step cycle: module deployed, runs Clouds software, idle capacity sold, network gets denser, and back to the next module being easier to justify.](/images/the-loop.svg)

The shape of it: we sell the module. It runs our software. The owner uses the capacity they need — and when they aren't using it, our software sells what's idle. That's what Clouds is for. It's the demand side: the thing that turns somebody's unused capacity at two in the morning into revenue for them, and into supply for everyone else on the platform. The owner stops being purely a consumer of compute and becomes a supplier of it.

That closes the circle this whole piece has been drawing. Every module deployed makes the network denser. A denser network makes the platform more useful. A more useful platform makes the next module easier to justify. Supply and demand stop being two customer bases and become one. And "who controls AI — a few centralized companies, or communities of users" stops being a position I hold in an interview and turns into a business mechanic: the capacity is owned by the people operating it, and they get paid when somebody else runs on it.

It also resolves the idle-draw problem honestly instead of hiding it. Dedicated hardware that sits partly idle is a bad asset. Dedicated hardware that sells its idle hours is a different asset. The software isn't a companion product to the datacenter — it's the thing that makes owning one make sense.

What I won't tell you is that it pays for itself. That depends on your site, your power price, your workload, and your utilization, and anyone quoting you a payback period before modelling those four things is selling you something. Ask me for the model, not the multiple.
## The unflattering version, on purpose
The thing I've changed my mind about most is how much of this work is telling people what we can't do.

When we looked seriously at regulated industries, the tidy pitch was data sovereignty — pick your region, satisfy the regulator, done. The real finding was messier. HIPAA doesn't require data residency at all; the actual blocker is that every gateway provider in the path is a business associate who must sign an agreement, and of roughly thirty decentralized networks we surveyed, exactly one will. Owning our own hardware fixes none of it.
That research killed a go-to-market I liked. I published it internally anyway.

There's a design for the mechanical half of that problem. If an agreement has to travel to thirty different companies, signing it should be built in rather than be an errand. The document gets stored so that changing even one character is obvious; the signature is tied to that exact document; and the customer can check both for themselves without taking our word for it — from the same command they already use to deploy. It's written up, and it's on the list. Nothing is built. And it wouldn't be the whole answer even when it is, because a better signing flow doesn't make an unwilling counterparty willing.

Same discipline everywhere else. We don't have SOC 2, ISO 27001, or FedRAMP. Choosing which country your data stays in works on some paths through our system and is quietly ignored on others — we found that ourselves, wrote it down, and stopped claiming it until it's fixed. During closed beta, through July 2026, we served 3,846 deployments across 38 testers; that's dated history from a database we wiped before open beta, not current traction, and I label it that way every time.

None of that is modesty. Infrastructure is a trust business with a very long memory, and the only durable advantage a small company has over a hyperscaler is that a person will answer you honestly. That advantage evaporates the first time you're caught rounding up.

So here's the direction, stated as intent and not as capability. I think we're the ones who end up building the first decentralized network that can genuinely carry regulated work — medical records, audited financials — with the signing built into the network itself rather than bolted on beside it. Not because compliance is interesting; it isn't. But the reason thirty networks can't sign the agreement a hospital needs is that nobody owns the place where such an agreement would live. Build it into the network and the problem stops being thirty phone calls and becomes a box you tick.

That's further along than it sounds. The architecture is worked out, the signing design is written, and we've picked where the payments settle — one of the most widely used public blockchains, which I'll name when I'm ready to. What we don't have is any of it running in production, or a single certification to our name. Ask me again in six months.
## What I'm betting on
That a future without decentralized AI is the dystopia everyone claims to be worried about, and that the people repeating the worry are mostly building the other thing.
That standards only bind when the people setting them also run the presses.
And that infrastructure is the least glamorous and most consequential place to make that argument, which is exactly why it's under-contested.
I started out trying to write the rules. It turns out the rules live in the layer underneath — so that's the layer I'm building.
Clouds. The future, deployed.
*Angela Steffens is founder and CEO/CTO of Alternate Futures. Olympia, WA. [alternatefutures.ai](https://alternatefutures.ai)*
